content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Soft-topK Token Pruning (STP) and Multi-layer Token Assembly (MTA) to address the segmentation problems. The authors reformulate segmentation as a sparse encoding → token completion → dense decoding (SCD) pipeline. Based on subset sampling, STP module can be flexibly incorporated into a standard ViT to prune tokens with greater efficiency while maintaining accuracy. On the other hand, MTA is to recover a full set of tokens, i.e., a dense representation, from a sparse set. MTA preserves high-detail information for accurate segmentation. Experiments show SCD pipelines equipped with our STP and MTA are much faster than baselines without token sparsification in both training (up to 120% higher throughput) and inference (up to 60.6% higher throughput) while maintaining segmentation quality.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
##########################################################################

Pros:

- The paper is the first to use token pruning/dropping for ViT-based segmentation, and the authors reformulate segmentation as a sparse encoding → token completion → dense decoding (SCD) pipeline, which is an interesting idea for the medical image segmentation area.
- The motivation of this paper is very clear, the authors propose two modules: Soft-topK Token Pruning (STP) and Multi-layer Token As- sembly (MTA) to fulfill sparse encoding and token completion respectively. i) In sparse encoding, STP predicts token-wise importance scores with a lightweight sub-network, thus avoiding the limi- tation of [CLS] token attention weights in segmentation. Then, STP always samples topK-scored tokens instead of making binary decisions per token separately, accelerating training because only the sampled tokens are involved in memory and computing.
- The paper is well-written and the comparison of benchmark methods is also interesting to read.
##########################################################################

Cons:

- I understand the problems in Sparse Encoding and Token Completion, but I'm curious why authors only evaluate the proposed framework on medical image segmentation datasets, is there anything special about medical images? It would be better if the authors could articulate more clearly the connection between the medical image case and the proposed method?
- The core module STP seems just added Soft TopK Sampling based on Gumbel Softmax Trick, and MTA seems just concatenated pruned tokens, such novelty seems limited?

content.title: Response
content.comment:
**Q1**: I understand the problems in Sparse Encoding and Token Completion, but I'm curious why authors only evaluate the proposed framework on medical image segmentation datasets, is there anything special about medical images? It would be better if the authors could articulate more clearly the connection between the medical image case and the proposed method?\
**A1**: Thank you for this excellent question regarding the motivation of our work. As we have shown in the Appendix Table 6 & 7, medical images show very high data sparsity with respect to the target tumors and organs. We thus hypothesized that dropping tokens for dense prediction might be particularly effective for medical images given the relative sparsity of targets.

---

**Q2**: The core module STP seems just added Soft TopK Sampling based on Gumbel Softmax Trick, and MTA seems just concatenated pruned tokens, such novelty seems limited?\
**A2**: To see further, we should stand on the shoulders of giants.
1. Although our STP shares a similar goal as Gumbel Softmax, we have demonstrated our simple change of the sampling algorithm from softmax to soft-topk leads to much higher training efficiency (x120) and better segmentation performance. STP also avoids the modification of the self-attention module itself while DynamicViT does not. 
2. In fact, we are glad that the reviewer thinks our MTA is simple. MTA can be treated as a spatially-adaptive skip connection. Compared with MIM, we prove empirically that MTA produces more informative representations leading to significantly better segmentation results. 
3. The significance of our work is justified by the failure of combining existing methods naively, i.e., DynamicViT/EViT + MIM. We believe that the simplicity and effectiveness of our STP and MTA modules are strengths of our work rather than weaknesses.

---

**Q3**: In the experiment section, the authors need to add more explanations about the dataset and model selection. Why did the experiment design this way? And the author only uses NaiveCombinationofEViT/DynamicViT+MIM as the only baseline comparison, lacking enough baselines to prove that the proposed method is really effective?\
**A3**: We regret the insufficient clarity. 
1. For token pruning, DynamicViT and EViT are two representative methods that represent two types of sampling methods, i.e., gumbel softmax sampling and the [CLS] attention-guided sampling. The other related token pruning methods basically all fall into the two bins. 
2. For token completion, as far as we know, MIM is the only method that performs token completion from an incomplete token set.

Therefore, we combine DynamicViT/EViT and MIM as our baseline.

---

**Q4**: This paper is only focused on the MEDICAL IMAGE SEGMENTATION CASE, is the proposed method can be generalizable? Can it be applied to general image segmentation scenarios?\
**A4**: We have built our method with Segmenter on ADE20K and Cityscapes. With a pruning ratio of 0.75, we observe a more obvious decrease in performance than in medical image segmentation tasks: (ADE20K (IoU: 49.60 -> 44.26) and Cityscapes (IoU: 80.6 -> 77.2\%). This is under expectation because ADE20K and Cityscapes contain denser targets than medical images.

---

**Q5**: Missing code link to reproduce experiments.\
**A5**: We will release our code upon acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors proposed a method for sparsely sampling tokens in the encoder of a transformer-based segmentation architecture. A prediction scoring module is developed to evaluate and keep only the top-k "high-scored" tokens, so the computational cost of the encoder could be largely reduced. For the token reconstruction during the decoder part, the authors proposed to utilize the intermediate representations of the dropped token to decode the dropped tokens. Decoder parts from the existing UNETR segmentation networks are adopted and integrated here. Two medical image segmentation datasets are employed here for the experiments. Superior results of the proposed method are reported in comparison to the other two sparse sampling strategies and other transformer-based segmentation methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ the manuscript is overall easy to follow. All parts of the proposed methods, e.g., STP and MTA, are clearly introduced.
+ A comparison to previous sparse encoding methods is conducted. 

Weakness:
- The proposed MTA module is mainly relying on the UNETR network, which utilizes the intermediate token representation for the final dense decoding. However, the concept is relatively common and has been widely used in the segmentation framework, e.g., the group of U-Net models. Therefore, the technical novelty of MTA is limited.
- There is some unclarity of the proposed STP module, which keeps only the top K "high-scored" tokens. How K is related to the gradient approximation process is not clear to me. As shown in Eq. 2, I did not see how K would affect the approximation. Does that mean the gradients are roughly the same, whatever K is chosen? More insights into this operation should be illustrated and discussed.
- Experiments of different K should be included, which are directly related to the computational cost of the encoder and the overall model performance. There are experiments on the pruning ratio. Are they related? And how?
- The employed data BTCV is less commonly used in the literature. I will suggest the authors take all the tasks in MSD (not only the brain tumor one) into the experiments. It will help better understand the benefit and weaknesses of the proposed method. 
- A simple baseline of the random dropping of some tokens at each level of the encoders could help understand the value of top-k scoring-based dropping. The comparison between MTA and MIM is less meaningful, considering tokens are missing in the input for the MIM setting, and its worse performance could be easily foreseen. 
- Common and latest segmentation frameworks should be included in the comparison, i.e., nn-UNet and Swin-transformer-based segmentation model.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of the manuscript is overall good. The proposed STP module is novel with the approximation of gradients in the top-k operation during the backpropagation, though it is not clearly introduced and justified. It will also be a bit tricky to build this component without accessing the codes.
content.summary_of_the_review: The overall quality of the presented work is good, though there is some unclarity of the STP module and a less novel MTA module. The performance gain is largely from the adopted UNETR model. Moreover, my main concerns are about the experiments, e.g., more extensive and more diverse datasets could be employed, and SOTA results on the datasets should be added. It also lacks insights and in-depth discussion of proposed STP modules, e.g., how and why the approximation works.

content.title: Response Part1
content.comment:
**Q1**: The proposed MTA module is mainly relying on the UNETR network, which utilizes the intermediate token representation for the final dense decoding. However, the concept is relatively common and has been widely used in the segmentation framework, e.g., the group of U-Net models. Therefore, the technical novelty of MTA is limited.\
**A1**: We respectfully disagree. 
1. MTA does not rely on any specific network. It can be combined with many existing segmentation frameworks.
2. We point out that the MTA concept is essentially different from UNet-style networks. Specifically, MTA first collects partial features adaptively from multiple layers. Since the collected tokens are ordered differently with different inputs, MTA needs to rearrange the concatenated multi-layer tokens before restoring the spatial dimension. In contrast, U-Net just concatenates whole feature maps from multi-layers.

---

**Q2**: There is some unclarity of the proposed STP module, which keeps only the top-K "high-scored" tokens. How K is related to the gradient approximation process is not clear to me. As shown in Eq. 2, I did not see how K would affect the approximation. Does that mean the gradients are roughly the same, whatever K is chosen? More insights into this operation should be illustrated and discussed.\
**A2**: 
1. In Eq. 2, different K values lead to different discrete $\mathbf{M}_i$. But the continuous $\tilde{\mathbf{M}}_i$ remains the same under different K values. 
2. Gradients are different with different K values. The gradient of the i-th token will be passed to its token score $s_i$ if token i is among the top-K. On the contrary, the negative gradient of the i-th token will be assigned to its token score $s_i$ if token i is outside the top-K. Thus, the scoring network needs to assign higher scores to the truly important tokens such that these tokens are more likely to be selected.

---

**Q3**: Experiments of different K should be included, which are directly related to the computational cost of the encoder and the overall model performance. There are experiments on the pruning ratio. Are they related? And how?\
**A3**: Actually, K is jointly decided by pruning ratio and total number of tokens. Here is the formula: $K = N_{tokens} \times (1 - r)$ where $N_{tokens}$ denotes total number of tokens and $r$ denotes pruning ratio. As for a specific task, $N_{tokens}$ is fixed. So K is decided only by the pruning ratio $r$. We have ablated over pruning ratios in Table 3.

---

**Q4**: The employed data BTCV is less commonly used in the literature. I will suggest the authors take all the tasks in MSD (not only the brain tumor one) into the experiments. It will help better understand the benefit and weaknesses of the proposed method.\
**A4**: 
1. We respectfully disagree that BTCV is less commonly used in the literature. In fact, [1][2][3] all demonstrate their methods on BTCV. 
2. We note that the baseline UNETR (patch_size=8) training can cost ~72 hours on a single A100. Therefore, it is unrealistic to demonstrate our method on all the MSD tracks. We will try to demonstrate our method on additional tasks in the future.

---

**Q5**: A simple baseline of the random dropping of some tokens at each level of the encoders could help understand the value of top-k scoring-based dropping. The comparison between MTA and MIM is less meaningful, considering tokens are missing in the input for the MIM setting, and its worse performance could be easily foreseen.\
**A5**: 
1. We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestion. We have experimented with the suggested random dropping baseline on BTCV with a pruning ratio of 90\%. All other experimental settings remain unchanged. The random dropping baseline achieves $76.62\% \pm 0.25$ DSC performance while ours achieves $82.18\% \pm 0.12$. The visualization in Figure. 2 also shows that our STP is able to select the tokens in or around the target. These all demonstrate the effectiveness of our STP module.
2. To our best knowledge, prior to our work, MIM is the only published work that completes a full token set from incomplete ones. Thus, it is natural and necessary to compare with it.

---

**Q6**: Common and latest segmentation frameworks should be included in the comparison, i.e., nn-UNet and Swin-transformer-based segmentation model.\
**A6**: Here is the comparison on BTCV:
| Method | DSC% |
| --- | --- |
| nnUNet | 86.99 |
| nnFormer | 86.57 |
| UNETR | 79.56 |
| Ours | 82.18 |

Our inferior performance to nnUNet & nnFormer is mainly caused by the difference in data preprocessing. We follow the same data preprocessing as UNETR while nnUNet & nnFormer adopt a different and more efficient data preprocessing pipeline. We will rebase our method on nnUNet-style data preprocessing in the future.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work develops and formulates the image segmentation based on transformer as a pipeline of sparse encoding, token completion, and dense decoding. It proposes the Soft-topK Token Pruning (STP) for the sparse encoding. For the token completion, Multi-layer Token Assembly (MTA) restores a full token sequence by assembling both sparse output tokens and the pruned intermediate tokens from multiple layers. It evaluates on 2 medical image segmentation dataset: the CT Multi-organ Segmentation dataset (BTCV) with 30 patients, and the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) with 484 patients. The proposed method achieves similar performance with UNETR while being faster in training and inference.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

-- Authors formulate the image segmentation as a pipeline of sparse encoding, token completion, and dense decoding. This scheme is able to alleviate the training burden/speed of transformer based segmentation network.

-- They propose the Soft-topK Token Pruning (STP) for the sparse encoding. STP trains a lightweight subnetwork to predict the importance scores of all the tokens (similar to DynamicViT), and select the top K tokens by relaxing the sampling of discrete top K masks to a continuous approximation, the Gumbel-Softmax distribution.

-- To recover the full set of token before entering the decoding, they simply assemble both the output sparse tokens and the pruned intermediate tokens from multiple layers. 

Weakness:

-- The novelty of this work is relative minor. The STP is similar to DynamicViT, with the difference of using a continuous approximation for differential to select the top K tokens.  The MTA is simply assemble both the output sparse tokens and the pruned intermediate tokens from multiple layers. 

-- The experimental results are not sufficiently convincing. (1) Authors used the two public datasets, BTCV and Brats. However, they only used the training data to divide as training/validation/testing, where they did not evaluate on the official testing data. (2) For the BTCV dataset, why only report 8 organs (instead of 13 organs) results in the experiment. It does not need to align with the organ number reported by Chen et al 2021.  (3) Lacks of comparison with the leading segmentation methods, e.g. nnUNet.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of this work is satisfactory. The novelty is more of incremental. The reproducibility seems fine.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
**Q1**: The novelty of this work is relatively minor. The STP is similar to DynamicViT, with the difference of using a continuous approximation for differential to select the top K tokens. The MTA simply assembles both the output sparse tokens and the pruned intermediate tokens from multiple layers.\
**A1**: To see further, we should stand on the shoulders of giants. 1) Although our STP shares a similar goal as DynamicViT, we have demonstrated our simple change of the sampling algorithm from softmax to soft-topk leads to much higher training efficiency (x120) and better segmentation performance (DynamicViT: 80.24; Ours: 82.18). STP also avoids the modification of the self-attention module itself while DynamicViT does not. 2) In fact, we are glad that the reviewer thinks our MTA is simple. MTA can be treated as a spatially-adaptive skip connection. Compared with MIM, we prove empirically that MTA produces more informative representations leading to significantly better segmentation results (MIM: 44.71; MTA: 82.18). 3) The significance of our work is justified by the failure of combining existing methods naively, i.e., DynamicViT/EViT + MIM. We believe that the simplicity and effectiveness of our STP and MTA modules are strengths of our work rather than weaknesses.

---

**Q2**: The experimental results are not sufficiently convincing. The authors used the two public datasets, BTCV, and Brats. However, they only used the training data to divide as training/validation/testing, where they did not evaluate on the official testing data.\
**A2**: We clarify our consideration and justify our choice of evaluation protocols below:
1. There is a considerable time gap between submitting to the test server and getting the test results, e.g., ~24hrs on BTCV. In addition, the MSD test server was also shut down for a period around May.
2. It is worth noting that BTCV and BraTS are both from past challenges. Splitting the challenge training dataset into train/val/test has been widely adopted in [1,2,3]. To guarantee the fairness of comparison, we use the same train/val/test sets with [1,2,3]. A similar routine can also be found in the famous ImageNet benchmark: researchers working on ImageNet usually only report the validation results instead of always evaluating on the test server.

---

**Q3**: For the BTCV dataset, why only report 8 organs (instead of 13 organs) results in the experiment. It does not need to align with the organ number reported by Chen et al 2021.\
**A3**: As we have introduced in Sec 4.1, our experiment setting is aligned with the experimental setting in [1] for the convenience and fairness of comparison. We provide the 13 organs performance of our method here and in Table 8 of the revised appendix.

---

**Q4**: Lacks of comparison with the leading segmentation methods, e.g. nnUNet.
**A4**: We provide additional comparisons on BTCV here: 
| Method | DSC% |
| --- | --- |
| nnUNet | 86.99 |
| nnFormer | 86.57 |
| UNETR | 79.56 |
| Ours | 82.18 |

Our inferior performance to nnUNet & nnFormer is mainly caused by the difference in data preprocessing.
